title: Pascal's night of fire
hookLine: on 23 November 1654, Pascal writes two hours of fire on paper and sews it into his coat (the Memorial)

lines: ONE NIGHT, ALONE IN HIS ROOM.
cards: Is there something you keep close without telling anyone? A note from someone who's gone, folded in your wallet. A screenshot you never delete.

A ticket stub in a drawer. The kind of thing people say they'd run back into a burning house for. Back on day ten we met Blaise Pascal, who said our unhappiness comes from not being able to sit quietly in a room.
Today: what happened to him one night, alone in his own room, and what, the story goes, he carried in his coat from then on.

teach.b: Pascal was a mathematician and an inventor.
On a Monday night, the twenty-third of November, 1654, something happened to him, from about half past ten until about half past midnight. We don't know exactly what.
What we have is what he wrote down right then, on a sheet of paper. It starts with a date and a time. Then one word, in capital letters: fire.

teach.h: NOT THE GOD OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.
teach.b: Then he wrote that the God he met that night was the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, not the God of the philosophers and the scholars. This from a philosopher and scholar.
Then, in broken lines, like someone out of breath: certainty; feeling; joy; peace. The word joy three times over, and tears of joy. He never published it, and as far as we know he never spoke of it.

The story told after his death is that a servant felt something stiff in the lining of his coat and found the page sewn there, and that he had moved it by hand each time he changed coats. It's called the Memorial.
For Pascal it was a meeting with God, the heart of his Christian faith.
For anyone, it's a picture of how to treat the few moments that matter most: not as content to post, but as something to keep close.

how: Christians who read Pascal treasure the Memorial as the record of his encounter with God; some people keep a copy of it, or a line of their own, close at hand in the same spirit.

the mathematician who kept his night of fire in his coat

games.q: you're Pascal. you've just lived two hours you can barely put into words, and you've written them on a single page. what do you do with it?

practice: Think back over your life for a moment that mattered: a night, a sentence someone said, a place where something became clear; not the most dramatic, the truest.
Find the fewest words that hold it, maybe just a date and one word, like Pascal's. If you like, write it on a small piece of paper and keep it somewhere close: a wallet, a pocket, a phone case.

wordCard.voice: Pascal. Two hours in 1654 that he wrote on a single page, sewed into his coat, and carried unseen until he died. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: keep it close. Not everything that matters has to be shown. Ninety days now.
